items.title: [science.org] Scientists map 607,000 vertebrate cells and a fly’s entire central nervous system
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have published two large-scale maps of nervous systems: a complete brain-and-nerve-cord wiring diagram for a fly, covering about 160,000 neurons and more than 200 million connections, and a body-wide cell atlas of the adult fish Danionella cerebrum, containing 607,370 cells. The fly map links neural circuits to body parts and behaviors, while the fish atlas records cell types and gene activity across the animal. The fish’s roughly 12-millimeter size made whole-body profiling possible. Researchers also used the atlas to track molecular changes during brain-tissue regeneration. The fly study found that many control circuits are organized as local sensory-motor loops rather than around a single central controller.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit. But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction, something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.

Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company, and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.

Surface temperatures there reached 30.06°C, and the anomaly rose to 3.48°C on Oct. 18 before easing to 3.34°C this week. items.title: [Fast Company] The Amazon rainforest, long known as the ‘lungs of our planet,’ now releases more carbon than it absorbs
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Amazon rainforest has long been called the “lungs of our planet,” because of how it takes in and stores billions of tons of carbon dioxide. 

But the Amazon has been losing that ability. Years of deforestation, drought, and fires have hindered just how much CO2 the rainforest can absorb. 

Now, the Amazon rainforest often releases more carbon than it takes in, a new study finds. It’s only in the “wettest years” that the rainforest is nearly carbon neutral.

The study, published in the journal Nature, was led by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research and included an international team of researchers. They used 15 years of atmospheric carbon measurements, which had been collected by research planes.

Those years were then grouped by different characteristics, like the level of human activities—which includes deforestation, logging, or using fires to clear land—and the amount of climate stress—like drought or heat waves. 

What the research found

Some years were wet with low human activity, some had low climatic stress but high human activity, and others had “intense global climate events, such as El Niño” along with intense amounts of human activity. 

In the years where the rainforest stayed relatively wet, and where there was relatively low deforestation and few wildfires, the Amazon was nearly carbon neutral. The forest was still a slight source of carbon into the atmosphere, but it “did not significantly contribute to the global carbon balance” in those years, the researchers write.

When drought or heat were mild but deforestation and wildfires occurred more, the net carbon emissions from the Amazon “jumped dramatically,” according to a statement. 

The years with lots of climate stress coupled with lots of damaging human activity were the worst. But they were still close to the net emissions from the second group, which led researchers to say that most of the carbon emitted by the Amazon comes from human activities, predominantly land-use change.

“Global climate and climate-mediated stressors are important modulating factors, but people’s choices about how to use and live on the land surface in this region are key to understanding the movement of carbon between the land and the atmosphere,” says coauthor Jen Johnson, assistant professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Kansas, in a statement. 

This isn’t the first paper to point out that the Amazon is not the grand carbon sink it once was. A 2021 study looked at how, as huge areas of the forest are cut down or burned, its ability to capture carbon was shrinking. 

In 2023, a year of extreme drought and high temperatures, researchers showed how the Amazon became a source of carbon emissions, releasing between 10 and 170 million tons of carbon instead of absorbing it. 

Slow burn

We’ve also long known that human activity is threatening the Amazon’s survival. In 2019, there were more than 74,000 fires burning in Brazil, mostly in the Amazon—80% more than the year before.

And though we often think of these as “wildfires,” they’re primarily set by ranchers who are clearing land for cattle to meet the demand for beef.  

The more deforestation, we know, the drier the Amazon becomes, which makes it even more difficult for the remaining parts of the forest to recover. 

“For many decades, there has been concern about the idea of a tipping point, where gradual drying and gradual loss of the forest could feed back on itself in a self-reinforcing way,” Johnson said.

“That could create a transition from an ecosystem type that has stored huge amounts of carbon in living vegetation to drier forests or other ecosystem types that do not store nearly as much carbon,” she continued. “The more carbon from the Amazon that moves into the atmosphere and stays there, the more trouble our climate system is in.”

Though the outlook is dire if these activities continue, the researchers say that policy changes can help. 

“There’s a clear, policy-relevant prescription that comes from this analysis,” Johnson said. “Measures to bring deforestation down to zero are required to manage net carbon emissions from the Amazon . . . It’s not something that’s out of our control because it’s being driven by global climatic factors—it’s something very much under the control of governments and individuals.”

items.title: [Kottke.org] Paleovirology: How HIV Started a Century Before Anyone Noticed
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

I’ve been vaguely aware for awhile that researchers had traced the origins of HIV/AIDS back to Sub-Saharan Africa. But I didn’t know the whole story, which turns out to be really fascinating.

For decades, one man was blamed for bringing AIDS to America. But the “Patient Zero” story was wrong. This is the story of how genetic detective work traced HIV’s true origins — from chimpanzees in Central Africa to a global pandemic — and how science unraveled one of the biggest myths in modern medicine.

Disappointingly, they didn’t list any of their sources for the video. I poked around a little and found a book called The Origins of AIDS that a Science magazine review called:

Extensively referenced, the well-written book reads like a detective story, while at the same time providing a didactic introduction to epidemiology and evolutionary genetics. As far as the origins of AIDS are concerned, unless some completely new evidence emerges, it will be difficult to come up with a better explanation than Pepin’s.

The YouTube comments are worth a read too, filled with remarks from those who lived through the early years of the pandemic or knew someone who did (or someone who didn’t).

Had a gay uncle who lived in San Francisco in the 80s and 90s. He would get so upset when he talked about HIV/AIDS. He lost so many friends to the virus. When I went to visit him in the 2000s, we visited 27 graves over the course of a weekend and laid flowers. Rest in peace to all those young people.

I worked in blood banking at Cedars -Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. It was policy to freeze blood samples from patients that expired due an unknown cause. Once the HIV test was approved the samples were tested and some were reactive to it. The samples were collected over decades, going back to the 1950s.

I have family who were foreign hospital workers in the now-DRC in the 1970s, where what we call AIDS was known as the Slims because of how the patients wasted away and died. People on the ground knew there was something going around, but they didn’t have the resources to figure it out.

Jazmyn Douillard with The Realm of Toys & The Nerd Room is extra happy for this year’s Downtown Trick r Treat in downtown Williams Lake. With Halloween falling on a Saturday, it was initially unclear if the annual festivities would be a go as many businesses, including professional services and government agencies, are closed on weekends. As it appeared there would be less than half the number of businesses participating from last year consideration was given to cancelling. Luckily for trick-or-treaters the decision was made to forge ahead with a total of 22 businesses, some only available for an hour or two, signing up to hand out candy and other treats. For years Douillard has organized the Downtown Trick r Treat annual festivities with her mother, Joan. She personally likes the 2 p.m. start time which is quiet, providing the perfect opportunity for toddlers, kids with sensory or sensitivity issues and anyone who might get overwhelmed to trick-or-treat before things pick up. She remembers the first Downtown Trick r Treat with about 15 locations signed up and running to Safeway to buy whatever she could to drop off after they ran out of candy in just 15 minutes. items.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.

Paleontologists have classified a fossil found in a Surrey clay quarry in 2001 as Paludohadros proudlovii, a previously unknown genus and species of plant-eating dinosaur that lived about 125 million years ago. The four-legged animal was about 5 metres long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 metric tons, but its bones indicate it had not reached adulthood. The fossil was donated to London’s Natural History Museum, where it remained for years before a detailed comparison with other iguanodontians revealed distinguishing features. The identification also helped researchers identify fossils collected from the same quarry in the 1950s as belonging to the newly named dinosaur. The research, led by Ricardo Sacamoto, a PhD student at the Natural History Museum and the University of São Paulo, was published in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology on Oct. 26, 2026. Sacamoto plans to continue examining the museum’s iguanodontian collection.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA ends Swift telescope mission after failed $30 million rescue
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

NASA has ended the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory’s science mission after the space telescope’s orbit fell too low for reliable observations and a private attempt to raise it failed. Swift made its final scientific observation on Oct. 20 and is expected to reenter Earth’s atmosphere in the coming weeks. NASA says most of the spacecraft will burn up, though some debris could survive. Launched in November 2004 for a planned two-year mission, Swift spent nearly 22 years tracking gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events. Arizona-based Katalyst Space’s LINK spacecraft was intended to capture the observatory and boost its orbit, but propulsion and attitude-control problems prevented the rescue. Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and observed more than 1,400 supernovae; its data have contributed to about 7,000 scientific papers. NASA is considering how to sustain rapid-response observations with existing telescopes and future missions.

items.title: [Kottke.org] Three-Body Orbits
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

There are no generalized solutions to the three-body problem. Say you have three planets orbiting each other: it’s impossible to calculate how they will move using Newton’s laws of motion and gravity.

Unlike the two-body problem, the three-body problem has no general closed-form analytic solution. The differential equations that govern the motions of three gravitating bodies are not integrable and cannot be solved to give explicit formulas for the positions of the bodies as a function of time. For most initial conditions, the dynamical system for three orbiting bodies is chaotic, and the only way to predict their motions is to estimate them using numerical methods.

But thousands of stable three-body orbits have been found — their paths repeat after a given interval. The Three Body Orbits website is an atlas of some of those orbits: you can watch each three-body system play itself out in a wide variety of different shapes and complexities. There’s this simple figure 8, this slightly less simple one, and this one that looks like a spirograph.

The site even enables you to search for new stable solutions to the problem in your browser. This is what one of my unsuccessful tests looked like — two of the planets locked in a gravity death spiral while the other one peaces out in the other direction:

items.title: [annahar.com] Scientists identify 66-million-year-old dinosaur adapted to eating fruit
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers identified Infernogallus jamesi, a turkey-sized, toothless dinosaur that lived about 66 million years ago and appears to have specialized in eating fruit and other soft plants. Its fossils, including a nearly complete skeleton, came from Montana and North Dakota. Its beak and jaw were adapted for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur with evidence of a specialized fruit diet. Paleontologist Greg Funston of Stony Brook University, lead author of the study published in Nature Communications, said the dinosaur's anatomy suggests a specialized feeding method. The researchers say it may have eaten berries and fleshy fruits; whether it helped spread large-seeded plants remains uncertain and requires more evidence.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Astronomers say ED138's dwarf-planet status awaits size measurements
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say 2026 ED138, an icy object beyond Pluto and a potential dwarf planet, cannot be classified until researchers measure its size more accurately. Its estimated diameter ranges from 600 to 1,500 kilometers, and Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, said the measurements may take months. The uncertainty arises because astronomers infer size from reflected sunlight: a small, bright object can appear as luminous as a larger, darker one. Infrared observations and longer-wavelength measurements with facilities such as Chile’s Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) could help narrow the size estimate; ALMA can detect light emitted by the object itself. If the body is large enough for its gravity to make it nearly round, it could qualify as the sixth dwarf planet recognized by the International Astronomical Union; the current size estimate alone does not establish its shape or status. Further observations will refine its size estimate, leaving astronomers and the Union to determine its classification.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Researchers report 2026 findings on parasitic fungi and brain tissue preservation
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers documented unusual biological and planetary findings in 2026, including animal tissues that survived outside a body for years and mouse brain slices that recovered electrical activity after cryopreservation. A study published in May found that fragments of scarlet sea cucumber tentacles and tube feet survived for more than three years in natural seawater. In March, researchers reported that neurons in rewarmed mouse brain tissue could fire and transmit signals across synapses. The work did not show that memories survived or that a mouse could be revived. Separately, James Webb Space Telescope observations of the rocky exoplanet TOI-561 b showed that it reflects roughly three-quarters of incoming starlight, with silicate-mineral clouds likely contributing to the effect. The planet orbits its star every 11 hours and reaches surface temperatures above 1,800 degrees Celsius. Researchers inferred the presence of an atmosphere from the planet’s reflected light and heat redistribution but have not established its composition. They say observations at longer wavelengths are a next step.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Canadian youth climate trial tests federal emissions policy and constitutional duties
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [agrarzeitung.de] Drought, heat and winter damage cut 2026 farm output across regions
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Weather extremes damaged crops and forage across Europe and South Asia in 2026, with drought and heat reducing yields and a cold winter with little snow harming Sweden’s autumn-sown grains. France’s sunflower harvest was estimated at 1.2 million tonnes, 14% below 2025, while Boerenbond estimated €260 million in losses for Flemish farmers and growers. In Baden-Württemberg, summer rainfall totaled 156 mm, about 45% below the 1961-1990 average; the state farmers’ association estimated forage losses at 30% to 40%, reaching 50% in the worst-hit locations. In Maharashtra’s Shevgaon area, drought has reduced fodder availability, while mechanized sugarcane harvesting removes a traditional source of green feed. Farmers say their livestock are producing less milk. Following late-September rain, Baden-Württemberg farmers are assessing whether grassland has recovered and whether reseeded areas will need further repair after winter.

items.title: [stuff.co.nz] Forecasters warn powerful El Niño could heighten drought and flooding risks
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The 2026-27 El Niño has strengthened across the tropical Pacific and is forecast to rank among the strongest on record, peaking during the Northern Hemisphere autumn and winter. The climate pattern increases the likelihood of drought in some regions and heavier rain in others, but does not determine local weather on its own. In the United States, forecasts point to warmer-than-average temperatures, wetter conditions in parts of the West and Southwest, and less rain and snow in the Pacific Northwest. California has already seen unusually high coastal water levels; a UC Davis report identifies low-lying roads, airports and neighborhoods at risk of flooding if high tides and winter storms coincide. Former officials and scientists warn that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has lost roughly one-fifth of its staff since January 2025, weakening its forecasting and response capacity ahead of the season. New Zealand’s outlook for November 2026 through January 2027 points to a greater likelihood of dry conditions in the north and east of the North Island and heavier rain in the south and west of the South Island.

items.title: [thestar.com] Canada fast-tracks $5.9-billion Vancouver port expansion despite whale concerns
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Canada has designated the $5.9-billion Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion in Delta, British Columbia, a project of national interest, moving its expected start of commercial operations forward by as much as four years to 2035. The proposed three-berth terminal would add annual capacity for 2.4 million containers and increase the Port of Vancouver’s container capacity by about 50%, as Ottawa seeks to expand trade and double exports to non-U.S. markets by 2035. The federal government says congestion without added capacity could drive shipping costs above $800 million annually by 2035. The designation gives the project certainty on remaining federal authorizations. Conservation groups say the terminal threatens salmon habitat and endangered southern resident killer whales; Ottawa says existing environmental conditions remain in force. Tsawwassen First Nation Chief Laura Cassidy conditionally supports the project but says the community still has concerns about the Fraser River estuary and Salish Sea. A final investment decision is expected by mid-2027.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [fortune.com] Canada and EU advance digital trade, mining finance and business links
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Canada and the European Union concluded negotiations on a digital-trade agreement and a competition pact at a Montreal summit on Oct. 30. They also agreed to support European Investment Bank financing for Canadian critical-mineral projects. The measures are intended to ease cross-border online sales and data flows, curb anti-competitive practices and expand financing options for mining. The two sides also agreed to give Canadian businesses and researchers access to European supercomputers. The measures are part of the new Canada-EU Alliance for the Future, launched by Prime Minister Mark Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. They build on the existing Canada-EU free-trade pact, which has already removed most tariffs. The two sides are also exploring faster transfers through linked instant-payment systems and expanded Canadian participation in Europe’s Erasmus+ exchange program. The EU has no existing process or defined cost for the proposed associate relationship. Canadian officials said talks on trade irritants tied to EU carbon-border and anti-deforestation rules were close to a deal, but no agreement had been reached. Carney said ministers and European commissioners would meet in March, with negotiations on the proposed relationship targeted for completion in June 2027.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Malicious JavaScript delivered through a website-monitoring integration sought to take over logged-in Polymarket traders’ sessions and redirect their assets, cybersecurity researchers said. Polymarket confirmed that a third-party provider was compromised and referred the incident to law enforcement, but did not publicly name the vendor. Researchers said the script read account data from browser storage, searched Polymarket’s application for its live trading client and signer, then attempted transactions using that existing access.
